a.answer: Ketoconazole requires an acid environment for its oral absorption
a.explanation: Azole antifungals (ketoconazole, itraconazole) are weak bases that require gastric acid for dissolution and absorption. Lansoprazole suppresses acid secretion, so ketoconazole plasma levels fall. This is the classic PPI–azole interaction.

Cimetidine inhibits CYP450 (CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP3A4) and therefore reduces the metabolism of warfarin, increasing its plasma level and the risk of bleeding. The other ulcer drugs do not meaningfully inhibit warfarin metabolism.

a.answer: Nabilone is derived from a psychoactive component of cannabis.
a.explanation: Nabilone is a synthetic cannabinoid derived from delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psychoactive component of cannabis. The other statements are false: gastric vagal afferents stimulate vomiting, 5-HT3 antagonists are ineffective in motion sickness, and NK1 receptor stimulation promotes (not inhibits) nausea.

a.answer: H. pylori infection in the gastric antrum reduces acid secretion.
a.explanation: Antral H. pylori infection typically INCREASES acid secretion (by suppressing somatostatin and raising gastrin), whereas corpus (body) gastritis reduces acid. The other statements about H. pylori are true.

a.answer: Metronidazole can be used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease.
a.explanation: Metronidazole is used in Crohn's disease (especially colonic and perianal disease). 5-ASA is poorly absorbed (not well absorbed), balsalazide releases 5-ASA + 4-aminobenzoyl-beta-alanine (only olsalazine is two 5-ASA molecules), and adalimumab is an anti-TNF antibody, not anti-IL-6.

a.answer: Bulk laxative use should be accompanied by drinking plenty of water.
a.explanation: Bulk-forming laxatives (methylcellulose, ispaghula) swell with water; adequate fluid intake is essential to prevent esophageal/intestinal obstruction. Lactulose is an osmotic laxative, and aluminium hydroxide causes constipation, not diarrhea.

a.answer: Loperamide decreases the gut residence time of the infective organism
a.explanation: This statement is FALSE (it is the incorrect one): loperamide slows motility and INCREASES gut residence time of the infective organism. Rotavirus is indeed uncommon in adults, kaolin is not recommended for acute diarrhea, and loperamide should not be used in dysentery.

a.answer: To decrease the occurrence of constipation or diarrhea
a.explanation: Magnesium salts are osmotic (cause diarrhea) while aluminium salts are astringent (cause constipation). Combining them balances the two effects, producing a more regular bowel habit.

IV H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine) are a standard choice for stress ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill patients. Sucralfate by NG tube is an alternative, but famotidine IV is the preferred regimen here. Ondansetron and misoprostol are not used for stress ulcer prophylaxis.

Ondansetron is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. 5-HT3 receptors are located on vagal afferent terminals that project to the nucleus tractus solitarius and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema) — these are its antiemetic sites. The other nuclei are not involved in emesis.

Methylcellulose is a bulk-forming laxative: it absorbs water into the fecal contents in the colon, promoting peristalsis 1–3 days later. Castor oil (stimulant) and magnesium sulfate (osmotic) act faster; docusate is a stool softener.

Lactulose is a non-absorbable disaccharide fermented by colonic bacteria to lactic/acetic acid, acidifying the colon and trapping ammonia as ammonium (plus osmotic diarrhea) — the treatment of choice for portal-systemic encephalopathy.

Chronic aluminium hydroxide binds dietary phosphate in the gut, causing hypophosphatemia (and aluminium accumulation with renal impairment). The other electrolyte changes are not typical of aluminium antacids.

Loperamide is a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor agonist that slows intestinal transit and inhibits secretion. It does not cross the blood–brain barrier to any significant degree, so it lacks central opioid effects.

For mild traveler's diarrhea without blood, bismuth subsalicylate is appropriate (antisecretory and antimicrobial). Vancomycin and erythromycin are not indicated; magnesium sulfate would worsen diarrhea.

Infliximab is an anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody used in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease that has failed 5-ASA and corticosteroids. Mesalamine adds nothing new, daclizumab is an anti-IL-2 antibody (not used here), and more steroid is not appropriate.

a.answer: Reaction with hydrochloric acid in the stomach lumen
a.explanation: Antacids are weak bases that chemically neutralize hydrochloric acid in the gastric lumen. They do not inhibit secretion, stimulate bicarbonate, or bind ulcer tissue (that is sucralfate).

Metoclopramide blocks D2 dopamine receptors in the CTZ (antiemetic) and in the upper GI tract (increases motility) — hence it both prevents nausea/vomiting and promotes gastric emptying. It also has weak 5-HT3 antagonist and 5-HT4 agonist actions.

Dronabinol (synthetic THC, a cannabinoid CB1 agonist) is added for breakthrough chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting despite ondansetron + dexamethasone + aprepitant. The other options are not antiemetics.

Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells release histamine, which stimulates H2 receptors on parietal cells. Famotidine is an H2-receptor antagonist — it inhibits the action of this ECL-cell product. Misoprostol is a prostaglandin analogue and sucralfate a mucosal barrier agent.

Metoclopramide is a D2 dopamine antagonist; blockade of pituitary/tuberoinfundibular dopamine receptors causes hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea, dizziness, drowsiness). Ranitidine, omeprazole and sucralfate do not raise prolactin.
Sodium bicarbonate is a systemically absorbed antacid: the bicarbonate load can cause metabolic alkalosis (and fluid overload). Calcium, aluminium and magnesium antacids are largely non-absorbable.

a.answer: Cimetidine decreased the clearance of theophylline.
a.explanation: Cimetidine inhibits CYP1A2 (and other CYPs), decreasing the clearance of theophylline and raising its plasma level → theophylline toxicity (nervousness, insomnia, palpitations, tremor). Ipratropium is not affected.

In renal failure (creatinine 4.5 mg/dL) magnesium- and phosphate-containing laxatives (magnesium hydroxide, sodium phosphate) must be avoided due to accumulation. Lactulose is osmotic, non-absorbable and safe; castor oil is not used daily.

a.answer: Discontinue bisacodyl, and increase fiber and fluid intake.
a.explanation: Prolonged daily stimulant laxative use causes dependence and loose stools. The correct advice is to stop the bisacodyl and manage constipation with fiber and fluids (bulk-forming approach).

Aprepitant is a selective neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist in the area postrema, blocking substance P — used mainly for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3, dronabinol is a cannabinoid, metoclopramide a D2 antagonist.

Acute dystonic reactions (torticollis, grimacing, oculogyric spasm) are extrapyramidal side effects of the D2 antagonist metoclopramide, especially in young patients. Ondansetron, scopolamine and dexamethasone do not cause EPS.

Docusate is a stool-softening (surfactant) laxative — gentle and safe in pregnancy. Castor oil and senna are stimulants (avoid in pregnancy) and bisacodyl is also a stimulant with limited pregnancy data.

For highly emetogenic chemotherapy (e.g., small cell lung cancer regimens), the guideline combination is a 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron) + NK1 antagonist (aprepitant) + corticosteroid (dexamethasone) — the gold-standard triple prophylaxis.

Palonosetron, a second-generation 5-HT3 antagonist, effectively controls cisplatin-induced emesis with a favorable cardiac safety profile. Droperidol and prochlorperazine prolong QT and can worsen cardiac failure; dolasetron also carries QT-prolongation risk.
Bismuth (e.g., bismuth subsalicylate, bismuth subcitrate) binds to tongue and gut bacteria, causing harmless black discoloration of the tongue and stools. The other drugs do not discolour the tongue.

Castor oil is a harsh stimulant laxative (ricinoleic acid) — not generally well tolerated (griping, dependence). Methylcellulose (bulk), polyethylene glycol (osmotic) and docusate (softener) are all gentle, well-tolerated laxatives.

Omeprazole (a PPI) inhibits CYP2C19, reducing conversion of clopidogrel to its active metabolite and thus its antiplatelet effect — an important interaction after myocardial infarction. H2 blockers (famotidine, ranitidine) and calcium citrate do not impair clopidogrel activation.
Extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia) are characteristic adverse effects of metoclopramide due to D2 dopamine blockade. The other drugs do not cause EPS.
Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analogue that stimulates uterine contractions and is contraindicated in pregnancy (abortifacient; category X). The other agents are safe in pregnancy.
Conventional H2-receptor antagonist therapy for duodenal ulcer healing lasts at least 4 weeks (with most ulcers healed by 4–8 weeks). PPIs heal more rapidly, usually in 4 weeks.
Cimetidine has antiandrogenic effects (binds androgen receptors, raises prolactin) causing gynaecomastia and impotence. Famotidine, ranitidine and the other drugs do not cause gynaecomastia.
Cimetidine inhibits CYP2C9/CYP3A4, reducing warfarin metabolism and increasing bleeding risk. The other ulcer drugs do not inhibit warfarin metabolism.

Meclizine is a first-generation H1 antihistamine (piperazine) used for motion sickness and for nausea/vomiting of pregnancy. Loratadine and fexofenadine are non-sedating (do not cross BBB); ondansetron is not first-line for motion sickness.
Docusate is a stool softener — it prevents/treats constipation rather than causing it. Diphenhydramine and promethazine (anticholinergic) and loperamide (opioid) all cause constipation.
Metoclopramide is the prokinetic of choice for diabetic gastroparesis: it increases gastric emptying by D2 antagonism and 5-HT4 agonism. Alosetron, cimetidine and loperamide have no prokinetic role.

Magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) is an osmotic laxative — non-absorbed Mg ions draw water into the lumen — suitable for verapamil-induced constipation. Aluminum hydroxide causes constipation; diphenoxylate and metoclopramide are not laxatives.

PPIs (esomeprazole) accumulate in the acidic parietal cell canaliculi where they are protonated to the active sulphenamide that irreversibly inhibits H+/K+-ATPase (the acid pump). Cimetidine is an H2 antagonist; the others are not acid-pump inhibitors.

Gastrin, histamine and (in this context) carbonate mineral waters all stimulate gastric secretion; pepsin is a proteolytic enzyme already present in gastric juice — it does not intensify gland secretion.
Alosetron is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist used for severe IBS with diarrhea; its main risks are severe constipation and ischemic colitis. It has no 5-HT4, D2 or NK1 actions.

Clarithromycin is a macrolide used in standard H. pylori eradication triple therapy (PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin or metronidazole). The other antibiotics are not part of standard H. pylori regimens.
Gastric acid secretion is stimulated by histamine (H2), acetylcholine (M3) and gastrin (CCK2). Serotonin is not a physiological stimulant of gastric acid secretion.

Misoprostol (PGE1 analogue) stimulates mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow — enhancing mucosal protection against damaging factors. Sucralfate is a barrier agent, bismuth subcitrate an anti-H. pylori coating agent, and omeprazole an acid suppressor.

Aluminium hydroxide is astringent and constipating (it also binds phosphate). Sodium bicarbonate and magnesium oxide are laxative/neutral; calcium carbonate can be constipating but aluminium is the classic constipating antacid.

Stimulant (contact) purgatives such as senna, bisacodyl and castor oil act by increasing intestinal motility and fluid secretion. Bulk laxatives increase non-absorbable residue, stool softeners alter consistency, and osmotics increase water content.

a.answer: It does not have antiandrogenic action
a.explanation: Ranitidine, unlike cimetidine, has no antiandrogenic effect (no gynaecomastia/impotence) and causes fewer CYP450 interactions. It is at least as potent and longer acting than cimetidine, with fewer CNS effects.

The acid-neutralizing capacity of an antacid depends on the equivalent weight (amount of acid a given weight can neutralize) and the rate at which it reacts with HCl. The pH of a 1N solution is not the governing factor.

Sucralfate requires an acidic environment to polymerize and bind ulcer tissue, so concurrent antacids (which raise gastric pH) reduce its efficacy. Antacids do not reduce the efficacy of cimetidine, colloidal bismuth or pirenzepine.

Syrup of ipecacuanha (containing emetine) is the classic emetic used to expel ingested poisons, acting both locally (gastric irritation) and centrally (CTZ stimulation). Apomorphine and emetine by injection are less dependable or obsolete.

Hyoscine (scopolamine) — a central antimuscarinic — is the most effective drug for short brisk journeys (rapid onset, potent). Promethazine theoclate and cinnarizine are also used but are more suited to longer/gradual exposure.

Metoclopramide increases LES tone and antral contractions but RELAXES the pyloric sphincter and duodenal bulb to promote gastric emptying. 'Increases tone of pyloric sphincter' is therefore the exception.

Cisapride (a 5-HT4 agonist prokinetic) was withdrawn because it prolongs the QT interval and causes serious ventricular arrhythmias (torsades) especially with CYP3A4 inhibitors like erythromycin and ketoconazole.

Liquid paraffin is a lubricant laxative — it does not stimulate the bowel, so it does NOT cause griping (colic). Its real drawbacks are interference with fat-soluble vitamin absorption, unpleasant taste, and lipoid granulomas/aspiration.

Stimulant purgatives are contraindicated in spastic constipation (irritable bowel with spasm) and intestinal obstruction because they intensify spasm. They are used in atonic constipation and bed-ridden patients.

a.answer: Breakdown of the drug in colon to release 5-aminosalicylic acid which suppresses inflammation locally
a.explanation: Sulfasalazine is split by colonic bacterial azoreductases into sulfapyridine + 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA/mesalamine), which suppresses inflammation locally in the colon — the basis of its therapeutic effect in ulcerative colitis.

b.modelAnswer:
1 – Erythromycin: activates motilin receptors on GI smooth muscle/enteric neurons → increases intestinal peristalsis (prokinetic).
2 – Omeprazole: proton pump inhibitor — irreversibly inhibits H+/K+-ATPase in parietal cells → inhibits 24-hour gastric acid secretion up to 95%.
3 – Mesalamine: a 5-aminosalicylic acid (salicylate) derivative used topically in inflammatory bowel disease.
4 – Aprepitant: neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist — antiemetic used primarily for chemotherapy-induced vomiting.
5 – Magnesium hydroxide: antacid that also has osmotic laxative properties.
6 – Misoprostol: prostaglandin E1 analogue with cytoprotective effects on the gastric mucosa (stimulates mucus/bicarbonate secretion, mucosal blood flow).
7 – Sucralfate: binds to necrotic peptic ulcer tissue and polymerizes in gastric acid to form a protective barrier over the ulcer bed, accelerating healing.

Apomorphine — a dopamine (D2) receptor agonist that stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) → vomiting within minutes of subcutaneous/IM injection; historically used to expel ingested poisons, though now largely superseded by gastric lavage and activated charcoal.
Alternative: Syrup of ipecacuanha — contains emetine and cephaeline; acts locally by gastric irritation and centrally on the CTZ; still occasionally used in poisonings but no longer routinely recommended (risk of aspiration, cardiac toxicity with overdose).

Erythromycin — a macrolide antibiotic that is also a motilin receptor agonist. It mimics motilin, increasing antral contractions and gastric emptying, hence its use as a prokinetic in diabetic gastroparesis. Mode of action: binding to motilin receptors on GI smooth muscle and enteric neurons → increased gastric motility and accelerated emptying; low doses are used to minimize antibacterial adverse effects.

Loperamide — a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor agonist that reduces the number of bowel movements by slowing intestinal transit and decreasing intestinal secretion (antisecretory). It does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so it has no central opioid/analgesic effects. Used for symptomatic control of traveler's diarrhea; contraindicated in dysentery (bloody stools) and acute ulcerative colitis.

Advise (chewable, safe in pregnancy): calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide — non-systemic antacids that provide rapid symptom relief without significant fetal exposure.
Avoid: sodium bicarbonate (absorbable → risk of metabolic alkalosis and fluid overload/edema in pregnancy) and aluminium hydroxide (causes constipation; aluminium may accumulate with prolonged high-dose use). Magnesium may loosen stools and calcium may constipate, so a combination often balances these effects.

c.modelAnswer:
a) Why O.M experienced nausea and vomiting (1 mark): Cyclophosphamide and vincristine are highly emetogenic cytotoxics. They damage gut enterochromaffin cells → release of serotonin (5-HT) and substance P, which stimulate 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and NK1 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone/area postrema → vomiting centre activation.
b) Planned antiemetic treatment before the first course (2 marks): triple prophylaxis with a 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron) + corticosteroid (dexamethasone) + NK1 antagonist (aprepitant) given before each chemotherapy cycle and continued for 4–5 days.
c) How they work (4 marks): Ondansetron — selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, blocks serotonin action on vagal afferents and in the CTZ/area postrema (acute emesis). Dexamethasone — corticosteroid that reduces prostaglandin release and central sensitization, effective against delayed emesis; potentiates the other antiemetics. Aprepitant — NK1 receptor antagonist in the area postrema, blocks substance P → prevents delayed vomiting.
d) Anticipatory nausea and vomiting (2 marks): give a benzodiazepine (e.g., lorazepam/diazepam) before chemotherapy plus behavioural therapy (relaxation, systematic desensitization); ensure maximal antiemetic cover so the conditioned response never becomes established.
e) Drug to relieve morphine-induced constipation (2 marks): an osmotic laxative (lactulose) or stimulant laxative (senna/bisacodyl) — or ideally a peripherally acting mu-opioid antagonist such as methylnaltrexone or naloxegol, which reverse opioid-induced constipation without affecting analgesia.
f) If methylnaltrexone: Mechanism of action — peripheral mu-opioid receptor antagonist that does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so it blocks opioid action on gut mu-receptors (restoring motility) while preserving central analgesia. Adverse effects: abdominal pain, flatulence, nausea/diarrhoea. Contraindication: gastrointestinal obstruction. (If senna is chosen: stimulant laxative activating colonic myenteric plexus; adverse effects — abdominal cramps, melanosis coli, electrolyte loss; contraindication — intestinal obstruction.)
g) Radical eradication of H. pylori (4 marks): 14-day triple therapy — PPI (omeprazole 20 mg BD) + clarithromycin 500 mg BD + amoxicillin 1 g BD (replace amoxicillin with metronidazole 400 mg BD if penicillin-allergic). Alternative: bismuth quadruple therapy — PPI + bismuth subcitrate + tetracycline + metronidazole. Confirm eradication with urea breath test/stool antigen 4 weeks after completion.

a) Cause of Crohn's disease (2 marks): Unknown/idiopathic — a chronic, relapsing, immune-mediated inflammatory bowel disease. In genetically susceptible individuals, an abnormal T-cell (Th1/Th17)-mediated inflammatory response to the gut microbiota is triggered by environmental factors (diet, infection, smoking) → transmural inflammation of the bowel wall.
b) Initial pharmacological therapy (2 marks): For mild-to-moderate colonic Crohn's — oral sulfasalazine or mesalamine (5-aminosalicylic acid, 5-ASA). If disease is moderate-to-severe, corticosteroids (prednisone) may be used to induce remission.
c) Mode(s) of action of the drug in (B) (2 marks): 5-ASA inhibits cyclo-oxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways → reduced prostaglandin and leukotriene (LTB4) synthesis in the colonic mucosa; it also scavenges free radicals and exerts a topical anti-inflammatory action on the inflamed mucosa.
d) Maintenance therapy (2 marks): Long-term mesalamine (5-ASA) to maintain remission; if steroid-dependent or refractory, add azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine (immunomodulator).
e) Mode of action of the drug in (D) (2 marks): Mesalamine — same topical anti-inflammatory mechanism as in (c) (inhibition of COX/LOX, ↓ LTB4, free-radical scavenging in the colon). For azathioprine — prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine → inhibits purine synthesis → ↓ lymphocyte proliferation.
f) Four adverse effects of the drug in (D) (4 marks): Mesalamine/sulfasalazine — nausea, diarrhoea, headache, skin rash; sulfasalazine-specific: reversible oligospermia/male infertility, folate malabsorption, rare agranulocytosis. (Any four correct.)
g) Alternative to reduce dependence on the drug in (B) (2 marks): If (B) was a corticosteroid — an immunomodulator (azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine or methotrexate) is the steroid-sparing agent; alternatively infliximab (anti-TNF) for refractory disease.
h) Mode of action and 2 adverse effects of the drug in (G) (4 marks): Azathioprine — prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which inhibits de novo purine synthesis → ↓ DNA synthesis and lymphocyte (T-cell) proliferation. Adverse effects: bone marrow suppression (leucopenia), hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, increased risk of infection, GI upset. (Any two adverse effects well described.)
